meta.title: GLP-1 Agonists Are Associated With a Significant Reduction in Breast Cancer Incidence in Women.
meta.abstract:
Purpose

Excess weight is a key modifiable risk factor for breast cancer. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1) promote weight loss and improve metabolic health, but their effect on breast cancer risk remains unclear.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study from January 1, 2022, to June 30, 2025, using electronic health records. We identified 217,624 unique women who underwent breast imaging; restricting to ages 45-80 years with a BMI ≥25 and a documented imaging outcome (n = 111,646; median age 61 years). The primary outcome was breast cancer detection. GLP-1 use was defined as a first prescription before the examination date and assessed in relation to race, ethnicity, age, and type 2 diabetes. To address potential confounding between these covariates and GLP-1 exposure, we performed one-to-one, case-control matching using propensity scores on the basis of age, race, ethnicity, highest BMI, breast density, and history of type 2 diabetes. The propensity matching to the GLP-1 use group was performed using the greedy nearest neighbor approach.

Results

GLP-1 exposure was associated with a lower incidence of breast cancer (odds ratio [OR], 0.649 [95% CI, 0.569 to 0.741]; P < .0001). In the matched logistic regression (30,528 observations; 600 cancer cases), GLP-1 exposure was associated with a lower breast cancer incidence (OR, 0.695 [95% CI, 0.590 to 0.819]; P < .0001).

Conclusion

In this large observational study of women undergoing breast imaging at a major academic center and affiliated sites, GLP-1 treatment was associated with a lower incidence of breast cancer, independent of age, race, ethnicity, BMI, breast density, and diabetes. The findings support the need for prospective trials investigating GLP-1 agonists for breast cancer prevention.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: Important established breast cancer risk factors were unmeasured and unadjusted (e.g., family history, parity, age at menarche/menopause, hormone replacement therapy, alcohol use). Furthermore, in the matched cohort (Table A2), prior history of breast cancer was lower in the GLP-1 group (5.9%, 907/15,264) than in the control group (7.8%, 1,197/15,264), and comorbidity distributions differed (Charlson 0-1 was 41.2% in GLP-1 vs 48.7% in matched controls), pushing the observed association away from the null.

findings.title: Uncontrolled reproductive, genetic, and lifestyle confounders
findings.mechanism: Key determinants of breast cancer incidence including parity, age at first birth, family history of breast cancer/BRCA status, and exogenous hormone therapy were not captured or adjusted for in the propensity model.
evidence: Covariates in propensity model were limited to age, race, ethnicity, highest BMI, breast density, and type 2 diabetes (Page 1342-1343).

findings.mechanism: A lower baseline prevalence of prior breast cancer history among GLP-1 users directly reduces subsequent breast cancer recurrence/new primary diagnosis rates in that arm.
evidence: Appendix Table A2 shows history of breast cancer was 5.9% (907/15,264) in the GLP-1 group versus 7.8% (1,197/15,264) in the matched control group.

domains.name: Measurement of the exposure
domains.direction_justification: Exposure was defined as any single prescription before the imaging examination date without requiring a minimum duration, adherence, or cumulative dose. Biological plausibility of breast cancer prevention from very short or recent exposure is improbable, creating protopathic bias and reverse causation.

findings.title: Crude exposure definition lacking duration and latency window
findings.mechanism: Patients with a single recent prescription immediately preceding imaging were categorized as exposed. GLP-1 agonists cannot plausibly prevent oncogenesis within days or weeks; individuals with preclinical cancer or symptoms may also have been less likely to be newly initiated on GLP-1 therapy.
evidence: GLP-1 agonist use was defined as a first prescription before the examination date (Page 1342); authors note 'we did not require a minimum duration of therapy' (Page 1347).

findings.title: Uncaptured out-of-system medication exposure
findings.mechanism: Patients obtaining GLP-1 agonists through compounding pharmacies or outside health systems were classified as unexposed controls.
evidence: Authors acknowledge potential ascertainment bias from prescriptions obtained outside the health system or compounding pharmacies (Page 1347).

findings.title: Prevalent user design and lack of new-user inception cohort
findings.mechanism: Classifying patients by any first prescription before an imaging exam combines prevalent and incident users without baseline washout, selecting for treatment-tolerant survivors and missing early adverse/outcome events.

domains.name: Selection of participants into the study
domains.direction_justification: Restricting the cohort strictly to patients who underwent breast imaging (111,646 of 217,624 imaged women) conditions on healthcare utilization and diagnostic evaluation. If symptomatic women or those undergoing diagnostic workup for breast masses had differential prescribing of GLP-1 agonists, collider stratification bias is introduced.

findings.title: Conditioning on breast imaging examination
findings.mechanism: The study sample is conditioned on receiving breast imaging within the health system. Diagnostic versus routine screening mammography indications were not separated, potentially selecting healthier GLP-1 patients into screening while controls included more diagnostic examinations.
evidence: Identified 217,624 unique women who underwent breast imaging, restricted to 111,646 with BMI >= 25 and documented imaging outcome (Page 1341, 1343).

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: No specific post-exposure co-interventions were identified that would systematically distort breast cancer diagnosis rates between matched groups.

findings.title: Standard post-imaging diagnostic care
findings.mechanism: Patients with abnormal imaging findings underwent standard biopsy/pathological evaluation irrespective of drug exposure.
evidence: Primary outcome was malignant breast pathology diagnosis during the study period (Page 1342).

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: A substantial portion of the original imaged population (54,799 excluded for BMI < 25 or missing BMI/outcome) was excluded during cohort derivation without detailed missingness modeling.

findings.title: Exclusion during cohort derivation
findings.mechanism: Complete-case filtering for BMI and imaging outcomes could introduce selection bias if missingness was related to health status or socioeconomic factors.
evidence: 54,799 excluded for BMI < 25 / undocumented outcome from 166,445 age-eligible women (Figure 1).

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: The outcome is malignant breast pathology diagnosis, an objective histopathological endpoint with low risk of misclassification.

findings.title: Objective pathological confirmation
findings.mechanism: Breast cancer status was determined by definitive malignant pathology diagnosis within the EHR.
evidence: Primary outcome was a malignant breast pathology diagnosis during the study period (Page 1342, Table 1).

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: Primary and subgroup analyses reflect standard matched logistic regression models conforming to the stated methods.

findings.title: Reported matched and unmatched predefined models
findings.mechanism: Odds ratios for matched and unmatched cohorts as well as subgroup analyses across race and diabetes status were reported consistently.
evidence: Matched OR 0.695 (95% CI, 0.590 to 0.819) and unadjusted OR 0.649 (95% CI, 0.569 to 0.741) reported (Pages 1341, 1344, 1346).

overall.summary: The study exhibits high risk of bias driven primarily by unmeasured confounding, crude exposure ascertainment without latency or minimum duration criteria (reverse causation/protopathic bias), and selection bias from conditioning the cohort on receipt of breast imaging. Matched controls had higher baseline history of breast cancer (7.8% vs 5.9%), and critical breast cancer risk factors (parity, genetics/family history, HRT) were unmeasured, artificially inflating the apparent protective effect.

baseline_comparability.summary: While GLP-1 users had greater systemic and metabolic comorbidity at baseline, unexposed controls had a markedly higher prevalence of prior breast cancer (7.8% vs 5.9% in the matched set), an unadjusted strong predictor that biases the effect estimate away from the null. This failure to match on personal cancer history explains a substantial portion of the observed protective association.
